reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Extremely rare autosomal recessive defect of ribose-5-phosphate isomerase (RPIA gene) in the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, one of the rarest reported inborn errors
Dominant feature is a slowly progressive leukoencephalopathy with developmental regression, seizures and peripheral neuropathy
Onset is typically in childhood with white-matter disease evident on MRI and characteristic accumulation of polyols on brain spectroscopy
Elevated ribitol and D-arabitol are found in body fluids and are markedly raised in cerebrospinal fluid and on cerebral magnetic resonance spectroscopy
The clinical course is remarkably slow compared with many leukoencephalopathies, sometimes spanning many years
No specific treatment exists, so care is supportive with management of seizures, spasticity and neurological disability
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating polyol accumulation (especially in CSF/brain) with confirmatory RPIA molecular and enzyme studies
reference.pathophysiology: Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase catalyses interconversion of ribose-5-phosphate and ribulose-5-phosphate in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. Deficiency disturbs pentose phosphate metabolism, leading to accumulation of the polyols ribitol and D-arabitol, which reach particularly high concentrations in the central nervous system. The resulting toxic or osmotic effects on the brain are thought to drive a progressive leukoencephalopathy with demyelination, alongside a peripheral neuropathy. Because the accumulated polyols concentrate in the brain, cerebral magnetic resonance spectroscopy is especially informative.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic leukoencephalopathies (e.g. metachromatic leukodystrophy, vanishing white matter disease)
Transaldolase deficiency and other pentose phosphate pathway disorders
Polyol pathway disorders causing white-matter disease
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to characterise the leukoencephalopathy
Cerebral magnetic resonance spectroscopy showing abnormal polyol peaks
Measurement of ribitol and D-arabitol in urine, plasma and cerebrospinal fluid
Nerve conduction studies to assess peripheral neuropathy
RPIA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Enzyme activity assay in fibroblasts where genetics are inconclusive
redFlags: Progressive developmental regression with an evolving leukoencephalopathy
New or worsening seizures alongside white-matter disease
Marked polyol elevation in cerebrospinal fluid or on spectroscopy
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive but often unusually slowly, with accumulating neurological disability over years; there is no curative therapy and long-term outcome depends on the extent of central and peripheral nervous system involvement.
pitfalls: Not requesting polyol analysis of cerebrospinal fluid or spectroscopy in unexplained leukoencephalopathy
Attributing the white-matter changes to a mitochondrial or acquired demyelinating cause without metabolic workup
Expecting a rapid course and dismissing the diagnosis because progression is slow
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of the Pentose Phosphate Pathway
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Supportive care only, as no curative or substrate-lowering therapy exists for this pentose-phosphate-pathway defect
Antispasticity treatment with agents such as baclofen alongside physiotherapy
Neurorehabilitation and symptomatic management of the peripheral neuropathy
Developmental and educational support with assistive devices for progressive disability
Serial brain MRI and magnetic resonance spectroscopy to monitor leukoencephalopathy and polyol accumulation
Genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive RPIA disorder
